extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of political theory, public opinion, and general educated readers interested in democratic theory
extracted.subtask_description: Chapter excerpt analyzing the conditions, assumptions, and institutional consequences of democratic public opinion in large modern polities, especially contrasted with the ideal of small self-governing communities. Emphasizes informational limits, institutional responses (checks, patronage, presidency, expert bodies), and practical failures of democratic stereotypes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal environment for democracy: small self-governing communities
rubrics_metrics.description: Democracy, as historically conceived by Jefferson and others, presupposes small, self-governing townships and farming communities where people 'managed their own affairs spontaneously' and where 'the ideal was at home.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the farmers are to manage their own affairs, they must confine affairs to those they are accustomed to managing; Jefferson disapproved of manufacture, foreign commerce, a navy, intangible property, and any government not centered in the small self-governing group. The ideal must be 'fenced off' from the abominations of the wider world to preserve spontaneous democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interests must be simple, intelligible, and easily managed
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If democracy is to be spontaneous, the interests of democracy must remain simple, intelligible, and easily managed.' Democracy requires that causes and effects operate within the region inhabitants know directly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conditions must approximate those of the isolated rural township so the supply of information can be left to casual experience; an extended, complex environment violates the premises of spontaneous democracy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-sufficiency and avoidance of entanglement
rubrics_metrics.description: Democrats favour Self-Government, Self-Determination, and Independence and aim to achieve self-sufficiency and to avoid entanglement with foreign contacts and complex external affairs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This preference explains tendencies in foreign policy (e.g., splendid isolation, Monroe Doctrine as a regional glacis) and domestic suspicion of manufactures and large cities which create external connections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Security is a necessary condition for functioning democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Security was seen as a necessity if democracy was to work: insecurity 'involves surprises'—people acting upon your life whom you cannot consult and novel problems requiring quick decisions incompatible with mass inertia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because democratic masses are slow to act, dangerous crises tend to require quick decisions by few people, a condition thought incompatible with democratic spontaneity; hence democracy prefers to minimize external dangers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of the omnicompetent citizen (rotation in office)
rubrics_metrics.description: The democratic stereotype assumes 'one man was as competent as the next to manage these simple and self-contained affairs'—the doctrine of the omnicompetent citizen—which in the township yields rotation in office and jack-of-all-trades public servants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This doctrine is practically true in small communities but breaks down when universally applied to a complex civilization, producing governance problems when specialized knowledge is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assumption of public-spiritedness and a homogeneous moral code
rubrics_metrics.description: In a self-contained community citizens were assumed 'consistently public-spirited and endowed with unflagging interest' and to share a homogeneous code of morals passed through 'school, church, and family.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under these assumptions disagreements would be limited to applying accepted standards to accepted facts and errors in reasoning would be exposed by free discussion; such assumptions do not hold in larger, diverse polities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formation of public opinion from stereotyped images and limited information
rubrics_metrics.description: Most citizens 'formed their picture of the world outside from the unchallenged pictures in their heads'—received from parents, teachers, a few feeble newspapers, pamphlets, speeches, religious training, and rumor—so public opinion was often based on 'casual fancy' rather than objective reports.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because few people have experience beyond their environment, public opinions are heavily stereotyped and little corrected by direct experience; this limits the reliability of popular judgments about translocal affairs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for instruments of knowledge: controlled reporting and objective analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Lawmakers cannot arrive at a true picture of the state of the union by assembling local impressions; 'He needs to know the local pictures, but unless he possesses instruments for calibrating them, one picture is as good as the next.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Like a factory head needing cost-sheets, the lawmaker needs systematic, controlled reporting and objective analysis—authorized instruments of knowledge—rather than a mosaic of anecdotal local pictures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balances as a remedy to neutralize local opinion
rubrics_metrics.description: The doctrine of checks and balances was devised to substitute 'the mild influence of the magistracy' for force and to 'deadlock local and class interest' so as to prevent them from obstructing national government.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constitutional devices were intended to enable government to control the governed and to oblige government to control itself; they were designed to neutralize the disruptive effects of self-centered communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patronage/rotation intended to democratize offices but producing a governing class
rubrics_metrics.description: Rotation in office and patronage were embraced as democratic reforms (and 'a sovereign remedy for political corruption'), yet in practice they founded a new governing class—professional politicians—oscillating offices between henchmen.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although patronage weakened parochial local spirit and helped stabilize the Union, it produced unintended institutional results (party organizations, a substitute governing class) contrary to the democratic ideal of citizen-rotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations of representative government in large polities (Congress as 'blind men')
rubrics_metrics.description: A congress of representatives is 'essentially a group of blind men in a vast, unknown world' because the constitutional theory relies on combining local wisdoms which are not a wide enough base for national policy, especially foreign policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without systematic means of information and analysis, legislatures must either have policy prepared by a few insiders and passed by partisan force or break policy into local items (tariff schedules, federal buildings) leading to logrolling and legislation tailored to local interests rather than coherent national policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presidential informational advantage and the one-sided relationship with Congress
rubrics_metrics.description: The President 'is in a position' to inform Congress because he presides over a vast collection of bureaus and agents, but 'he tells Congress what he chooses to tell it' and censorship of what is compatible with the public interest is in his hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This creates a 'one-sided and tricky relationship' where Congress must rely on leaks, newspaper enterprise, or subordinate indiscretions to obtain important documents; the President's informational edge can skew national decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Congressional investigations and expert bodies as imperfect substitutes for continuous information
rubrics_metrics.description: Congressional investigations are described as a 'legalized atrocity' that often yield little and where Congressmen, 'starved of their legitimate food for thought, go on a wild and feverish man-hunt.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better substitutes are systematic expert bodies and commissions (e.g., Interstate Commerce Commission, Federal Trade Commission, Tariff Commission) whose involvement represents a new and useful practice for assisting Congress with information and analysis; reliance on ad hoc investigations is a poor remedy.
